Q: Why we need Classes and Object when be have Functions? A:

I don't think the OP is arguing that OOP is useless. They are using Python, and based on their post, it seems procedural programming is doing the trick for them. They just want to understand more about OOP, because maybe they might choose it for certain problems.

Q: Possible race in TIdUDPServer.CloseBinding: listener thread keeps raw Binding reference while CloseBinding closes it before WaitFor A:

TIdThread.Stop only sets the stopped/terminated state. It does not wait for the thread to finish. WaitFor is called only after LListener.Binding.CloseSocket.

Correct. The listener thread may be in a blocked socket state waiting for the next client packet to arrive. The thread is signaled to stop, and then the socket is closed directly to cancel any pending socket operations, freeing up the thread to finish terminating itself.

TIdUDPServer.Bindings owns the TIdSocketHandle objects.

Yes.

TIdUDPListenerThread stores a non-owning FBinding reference to one of them.

Yes.

CloseBinding locks only the listener list, not the binding lifetime.

Yes. Because it is merely iterating the list of binding objects, which does not affect their lifetime. And besides, the iteration is inside the list lock anyway, so the lifetimes are already effectively being extended during the iteration, because you can't add/remove items while the list is locked.

TIdSocketHandle.CloseSocket locks the socket handle fields of a live object, but it does not pin the lifetime of the TIdSocketHandle object itself.

Yes, because it does not need to (not to memtion, there is no object lifetime pinning in Delphi/Pascal anyway). The assumption being that the binding object is not freed from memory while CloseSocket is still running on it.

The listener thread may still run AfterRun and touch FBinding while the owner thread is already in CloseBinding.

That is fine. CloseSocket() has an internal thread lock around its underlying socket field.

In an instrumented run I saw a listener that was created with a valid socket handle, then during shutdown its FBinding.Handle became a garbage value before the AV:

That should not be possible given the steps you outline. One thread would call CloseSocket, enter the lock, close the socket and set it to INVALID_SOCKET, and leave the lock. The other thread would call CloseSocket(), enter the lock, see INVALID_SOCKET and do nothing, and leave the lock.

What you describe sounds more like possible memory corruption is happening outside of the UDP server itself, and the server is just a victim of it.

If both threads reached the same live TIdSocketHandle, FConnectionHandle inside TIdSocketHandle.CloseSocket should serialize the close.

Yes.

The problem appears to be that the listener's FBinding reference is no longer a coherent live binding object by the time shutdown code uses it.

That should not be possible since the TIdUDPServer.Bindings objects are not freed during server shutdown. The Bindings must outlive the listeners. That is why the listeners use non-owning references.

Is TIdUDPServer.CloseBinding intended to be safe under rapid Active := False / Active := True cycles?

Yes.

Is the ordering in CloseBinding correct?

Yes.

In particular, should it call LListener.Binding.CloseSocket before LListener.WaitFor

No, otherwise a deadlock could occur if the listener is blocked on a socket operation. The WaitFor waits for the listener thread to fully terminate, but the listener would not see the stop request until its current iteration of socket operations is finished. That is why the socket is closed before the WaitFor. That will give socket operations a chance to cancel/fail so the listener thread can stop itself.

while the listener thread can still execute AfterRun and use FBinding?

That is perfectly fine for it to do.

Is there an official Indy workaround?

No, because there is nothing to workaround. This has been working fine for many years. You need to debug your issue deeper. It is likely not a problem in Indy itself.

avoid auto-created dual IPv4/IPv6 bindings and explicitly create one binding;

That has nothing to do with shutdown handling.

never clear/change Bindings after activation;

You can't change the Bindings while the server is active. But it is perfectly safe to do so after deactiving it first.

serialize Active changes externally;

You should be doing that anyway. You can't have multiple threads activating/deactivating the server at the same time.

patch CloseBinding to stop/wake/wait in a different order.

The order is not the problem.

Q: Is there way to detect that the upload documents are tempered(edited) or not. i am making an detection system for a org they need to find edited doc A:

As per my knowledge, there is no reliable way to determine whether an image or PDF has been edited in the general case.

The real question you should think of is "what kind of editing you want to detect":

For Example:

  • Metadata changes (Photoshop, GIMP, Word, etc.) : inspect EXIF/image metadata or PDF metadata using libraries such as Pillow, ExifTool, or PyPDF2.

  • Image manipulation/tampering (objects added, removed, copied) : use image forensics techniques such as:

    • Error Level Analysis (ELA)

    • Copy-move forgery detection

    • Noise inconsistency analysis

    • Deep-learning-based forgery detection models

  • Document modifications : compare against the original document using hashes, digital signatures, or content comparison.

For Python, some useful open-source tools/libraries are:

  1. Pillow (image metadata and processing)

  2. opencv-python

  3. scikit-image

  4. PyPDF2

  5. pikepdf

  6. exiftool

Also if this is for an organization handling fraud detection, the most robust approach is usually:

  1. Require digitally signed PDFs/documents whenever possible.

  2. Validate signatures and document hashes.

  3. Use forensic/ML checks only as a risk signal, not as proof of tampering.

Now a days scanned document, screenshot, print-and-rescan, or metadata removal can make edit detection extremely difficult. Even state-of-the-art AI models cannot guarantee whether a document has been edited, they can only provide a probability of tampering.

Q: System.Runtime, Version=4.2.1.0, PublicKeyToken=b03f5f7f11d50a3a has a higher version than referenced assembly A:

I had same problem. When I added the Views folder from the solution to the publish folder then the problem went away. For some reason Razor requires these source files to be present in the server AND up-to-date even when it compiles them also into .dll. Therefore it is strange indeed that the Views folder is not automatically copied during publish.

I personally made a junction like this
junction "MyProject\bin\Release\netcoreapp2.1\linux-x64\publish\Views" "MyProject\Views"

Alternatively, disabling the following line might help (have not tested but this issue seems to be related since in earlier versions of Net.Core there was no Razor compilation).

<RazorCompileOnBuild>true</RazorCompileOnBuild>
to
<RazorCompileOnBuild>false</RazorCompileOnBuild>

Q: Could not load file or assembly 'System.Runtime, Version=4.2.1.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=b03f5f7f11d50a3a' A:

To solve the problem, I originally guessed that System.Runtime.dll should be in .NET Framework Dll Folder, because on the NuGet page for this DLL, the version history doesn't contains 4.2.1.0, but after reading Scircia's answer, I tried to add the latest NuGet System.Runtime.dll to the project:

Right Click On Project > Property Page > References > Add.

The NuGet version of the DLL is 4.3.1, but its DLL version is 4.6.27406.3.

After adding, a new error shows:

Assembly 'XXXX(It's secret), Version=x.x.x.x, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=xx' uses 'System.Runtime, Version=4.2.1.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=b03f5f7f11d50a3a' which has a higher version than referenced assembly 'System.Runtime, Version=4.0.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=b03f5f7f11d50a3a'

But the DLL I added is 4.6.27406.3, so why did I get this 4.0.0.0 error? I finally found the main cause: in the project many components use .NET Framework 3.5, so it should be run at 3.5, but when I Right Click On Project > Property Page > Build > Target Framework, it shows currently use 4.0.

So I followed these steps to change the Target Framework from 4.0 to 3.5. I click OK, then again from 3.5 to 4.0, then the error was resolved.

That is, through 4.0 > 3.5 > 4.0, the web.config is auto modified and seems some DLL that needs 3.5 is removed, become a real 4.0, and in Framework 4.0 the System.Runtime.dll works.

Since it says it needs 4.2.1.0, but I added 4.6.27406.3, I suppose that using a higher version than 4.2.1.0 is allowed.

Q: Cycle detection with recursive subquery factoring A:

From the documentation on CONNECT_BY_ISCYCLE:

The CONNECT_BY_ISCYCLE pseudocolumn returns 1 if the current row has a child which is also its ancestor

and that on CYCLE:

A row is considered to form a cycle if one of its ancestor rows has the same values for the cycle columns.

In your example, row 2 does have a child which is also its ancestor, but its id has not been returned yet.

In other words, CONNECT_BY_ISCYCLE checks the children (which are yet to be returned), while CYCLE checks the current row (which is already returned).

CONNECT BY is row-based, while recursive CTEs are set-based.

Note that Oracle's documentation on CYCLE mentions "ancestor row". However, generally speaking, there is no concept of an "ancestor row" in a recursive CTE. It's a set based operation which doesn't nessessarily deal with trees. The anchor part and the recursive part can even use different tables.

Since recursive CTEs are usually used to build hierarchy trees, Oracle decided to add a cycle check. But due the set-based way the recursive CTEs operate, in general, it's impossible to tell whether the next step will generate a cycle, nor even does the concept of a "cycle" always make sense.

To perform the "next" step, the whole "current" set needs to be available. But to generate the current set (including the cycle column), we need to have the results of the "next" step. In other words, we can't generalize cycle detection without introducing cycles in the first place, so the cure would be worth than the disease.

CONNECT BY is a degenerate case of a recursive CTE. Its "current set" always consists of a single row, and its analog of the anchor part always references a single row in the same table. This way, the concept of an "ancestor row" is clearly defined, and cycle detection doesn't pose any problems.

I haven't looked into Oracle 11 and I'm not sure how they work around this problem.

SQL Server implements recursive CTEs just by disguising a CONNECT BY operation in CTE syntax. It requires placing numerous restrictions on what you can use in the recursive part of the CTE: no outer joins, no TOP, no CROSS APPLY, and so on. All these restrictions effectively ban operations that don't distribute over UNION ALL.

PostgreSQL's implementation, on the other hand, is truly set-based: the recursive part can refer to the anchor part and do anything with it. It doesn't have any means to detect cycles, though, because they're not defined in the first place.

Ironically, I received an email today on this very subject, which I will cover in my blog.

Update:

Recursive CTE's in SQL Server are nothing other than CONNECT BY in disguise. See this article in my blog for shocking details:

  • SQL Server: are the recursive CTE’s really set-based?
